sources.citation: E. Colin Cherry (1953). Some Experiments on the Recognition of Speech, with One and with Two Ears. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.
sources.notes: Foundational primary study (1953) in The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America establishing the core experimental paradigm and quantitative parameters.

sources.citation: E. Colin Cherry, W. K. Taylor (1954). Some Further Experiments upon the Recognition of Speech, with One and with Two Ears. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.
sources.notes: Measures interaural attention-switching time dips when speech alternates rapidly between left and right ears.

sources.citation: Davide Castelvecchi (2015). 3D-printed device helps computers solve cocktail-party problem. Nature.
sources.notes: Subsequent empirical and theoretical investigation (2015) in Nature extending the foundational findings.

sources.citation: Neville Moray (1959). Attention in Dichotic Listening: Affective Cues and the Influence of Instructions. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
sources.notes: Neville Moray's landmark dichotic-listening experiment demonstrating that a listener's own name breaks through an unattended ear channel.

sources.citation: Josh H. McDermott (2009). The cocktail party problem. Current Biology.
sources.notes: Subsequent empirical and theoretical investigation (2009) in Current Biology extending the foundational findings.

sources.citation: Patrik Wikman, Artturi Ylinen, Miika Leminen, Kimmo Alho (2022). Brain activity during shadowing of audiovisual cocktail party speech, contributions of auditory–motor integration and selective attention. Scientific Reports.
sources.notes: Subsequent empirical and theoretical investigation (2022) in Scientific Reports extending the foundational findings.
